course_description:
In this course students will critically reflect on the broad scope of anthropological inquiry by engaging with a range of advanced topics.

This is a course that invites students to engage with a range of research, theory and writing at the "front edge" of the discipline of anthropology. What does contemporary work tell us about the anthropology of the future, a future that advanced students in the discipline are already playing a part in defining? This course examines work in ecological, political and economic anthropology (in particular). We read an ethnographic book as our central focus, picking up on its conceptual, methodological and substantial questions, and we use other scholarly material to engage critically with topics related or parallel to the topics covered in the focus ethnography.ﾠﾠ

Students access weekly online short (20-30 minute) lectures, undertake independent reading and research, and use these to prepare for participation in face to face seminars and workshops.

The course will assist students to draw on what they have learnt in their undergraduate anthropology program and consider how the ideas will contribute to their own futures. It will support students to work through understanding what kinds of questions anthropologists commonly ask; how research achieves effective engagement with different actors; and, conceptual material that projects the discipline into questions of the future. A focus on engaged and scholarly research examines anthropology’s contribution to knowledge of human societies and role in cross-disciplinary debates. The course will prepare students to use their anthropological knowledge after their undergraduate degree, especially in terms of the communication skills practiced in seminar discussions and the analytical skills in writing critical literature summaries, both important aspects of pitching project proposals in applied (e.g. government, Non-govt and corporate ﾠprojects) and scholarly (e.g. research proposals) contexts.

course_aims:
This course aims to further students’ understanding of anthropology, examining recent developments and looking to the discipline's future. A key aim is to address how the development of anﾠanthropological perspective can informﾠa range of future endeavours students may take up their lives,ﾠinﾠemployment and future academic pursuits.

As a third year compulsory course in the Anthropology major, the course aims to deepen student’s grasp of concepts as these have been developed in the discipline and provide opportunities to practice engaging with these ideas in critical and productive ways.

learning_outcomes.description: Communicate effectively on contemporary conceptual and methodological knowledge in anthropology and its relevance to other disciplines and the world.
Apply advanced skills in critically reviewing anthropological literature, analysing case studies, and considering the positionality of researchers.
Identify an area or areas of anthropological knowledge to which you seek to contribute in future work or study.

assessment_details.title: Leading seminar discussion
assessment_details.task_description: During the first class each student will choose one week to be responsible for leading the seminar discussion Lead the seminar in class (ONCE – see schedule for “*student-led”): detail ONE work listed & raise 1-2 class discussion questions that show you have read all material. Oral presentation (5-7 mins) + MUST provide notes in hard copy at beginning of the class. Your notes for the discussion should show: A very brief summary of key reading – what is the material essentially about (in 1-2 concise sentences)? What is the author’s central argument, or the argument you find most compelling? What key points from this reading assist us to consider a broader topic/concept? What further questions are raised by the author/s for considering the topic/concept? (reference related literature) Draft 1-2 questions designed to generate class discussion of the reading and topic. Marking criteria and/or marking rubrics are available in the ‘Assessment’ folder in Blackboard for this course. Students are assessed as follows: Notes handed in at beginning of seminar; comprehension of the material, good summary of central argument and key points; a well drafted and considered question for class discussion; clearly spoken, keeping to time and engagement of other students throughout class time. NOTE: IF A STUDENT IS UNWELL they may arrange to lead the seminar on an alternative day. They must be in touch before the class to notify the course coordinator and arrange an alternative. AI Use: This assessment task evaluates student’s abilities, skills and knowledge to read and consider the literature. AI tools that summarise the literature may be used to generate key points, but students should be aware that these tools often miss the subtleties of argument, may misrepresent authors' ideas or not provide you with enough knowledge to devise good questions for discussion. A failure to reference AI use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. Students must complete an AI usage declaration and submit it with their assessment. Additional resources are available through UQ AI Student Hub . Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.title: Essay
assessment_details.other_conditions: Student specific. See the conditions definitions
assessment_details.task_description: 2800 words: Self devised essay question. Self devised research question, based on course material OR Students may focus on a topic they are passionate about and which they may wish to explore further as part of a focus of life, recreational interests, or future study (an Honours thesis?). The final essay asks you to devise your own critical question and then explore debates that inform that question using the conceptual or theoretical literature in anthropology. Students are encouraged to choose their topic early in the semester and read accordingly. In week 10 students declare their topic and outline the draft question. This is assessed (5%). Week 10 is also an opportunity to discuss your essay topic, planning and development and gain some feedback. learning_activities.topic: What is theory and how might anthropological theories prepare us for the future? See Blackboard for weekly activity schedule. Course overview and workshop: How to write a critical question arising from a summary. How to participate & ask discussion questions. Each student will introduce themselves by identifying a topic of interest in anthropology and nominating a week for leading discussion. ALSO 1. Examine Tsing’s opening pages – what are we in for? 2. Raise questions about the history of anth. theory (Ortner). Consider what constitutes theory (Million’s) and ‘critique’. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

The different elements of ethnographic theory Detailed instructions on weekly critical questions assessment. **Use of AI – discussion and guidelines. Read TSING and ONE OTHER introduction chapter and summarise. How do these different ethnographies compare as works of theorising about human worlds? What questions are asked? *student led* Critical questions 1 Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

The local and global frontiers of coloniality: who makes theory? How are frontiers both local and global and what do they tell us of colonial orders? What might it mean, in particular, to decolonise anthropological theory? *student led* Critical questions 2 Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Extractive economies and scales of finance How does global capitalism operate to create different scales and realities? Discuss scale, “modularity” and the operation of “global actors”. *student led* Critical questions 3 Learning outcomes: L01, L02
Futures, deep reading and critical thinking (Online only) Online only class – considering futures, questions on ‘ethical use’ of AI. Catch up on reading for next module. Learning outcomes: L01, L02

Classifications and cosmopolitan natures What are the implications of the category “Nature” for different people, and for anthropological theory? Consider nature and culture: what and who belongs in which categories? *student led* Critical questions 4 Learning outcomes: L01, L02

Local natures and nature rights How do global categories get localised and can the reverse be true? Discuss the idea of conservation put to work in conservation and movements for ‘nature rights’. *student led* Critical questions 5 Learning outcomes: L01, L02

Weeds and multispecies relations Discuss ideas of non-human, or ‘more-than-human’ beings and agency. What might attention to inter-species relations reveal? What kinds of ethnographic thinking led to the consideration of “multispecies anthropology”? *student led* Critical questions 6 Learning outcomes: L01, L02
‘Post conventional anthropology’ Guest, Prof Amanda Kearney * student led – read Kearney + one other article to inform discussion Learning outcomes: L01, L02

Agency, power and making change ESSAY WORKSHOP: How do I think anthropology into a good ethnographic research question? Students must declare essay topic and discuss the draft (5% of final mark). (5% of final mark: students must declare and discuss their essay question) Learning outcomes: L01, L02

Social movement: Agency, power and making change Resistance and other social movements have long held fascination for anthropologists. What counts as resistance and is it an effective diagnostic of power? *student led* Critical questions 7 Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Ethical futures, the Anthropocene and ‘the community’ In what way is the work of conservation a kind of cosmopolitics? Who and what counts as community in a ‘sustainable future’? *student led Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
Final Essay check-in class Learning outcomes: L01, L02
